claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings regarding half-life and methaemoglobin associations.

claims.claim: Tafenoquine is the first new drug licensed for radical treatment of relapsing malaria in 70 years.
claims.source: Tafenoquine is a newly licensed 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial drug for the radical treatment of relapsing Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale malarias; the first for 70 years.
claims.evidence: This is stated as historical context in the introduction.

claims.claim: Tafenoquine is eliminated slowly and can be given as a single dose for radical cure.
claims.source: Tafenoquine is eliminated slowly and can be given as a single dose for radical cure or as weekly chemoprophylaxis (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019; Lacerda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited clinical trial publications.

claims.claim: Tafenoquine can be given as weekly chemoprophylaxis.
claims.source: Tafenoquine is eliminated slowly and can be given as a single dose for radical cure or as weekly chemoprophylaxis (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019; Lacerda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited clinical trial publications.

claims.claim: Tafenoquine provides a substantial operational advantage over primaquine which needs to be given at least once daily for 7-14 days.
claims.source: This provides a substantial operational advantage over the currently recommended radical treatment, primaquine, which is eliminated rapidly and needs to be given at least once daily for 7–14 days (Nekkab et al., 2021; Taylor et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on dosing regimen differences, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Primaquine is metabolised rapidly to carboxyprimaquine which is considered pharmacologically inert.
claims.source: Primaquine is metabolised rapidly to carboxyprimaquine (considered pharmacologically inert) and, through a different pathway, to a series of reactive oxidative intermediates which are thought to be responsible for both antimalarial activity and haemolytic toxicity (Camarda et al., 2019; White et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about primaquine metabolism supported by citations.

claims.claim: Primaquine is metabolised to reactive oxidative intermediates thought to be responsible for both antimalarial activity and haemolytic toxicity.
claims.source: Primaquine is metabolised rapidly to carboxyprimaquine (considered pharmacologically inert) and, through a different pathway, to a series of reactive oxidative intermediates which are thought to be responsible for both antimalarial activity and haemolytic toxicity (Camarda et al., 2019; White et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The main limitation in implementing antimalarial 8-aminoquinolines is oxidative haemolysis.
claims.source: The main limitation in implementing the antimalarial 8-aminoquinolines is oxidative haemolysis.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the drug class.

claims.claim: Haemolysis can be life-threatening in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
claims.source: Haemolysis can be life-threatening in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, which is very common in malaria endemic areas (Recht et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: G6PD deficiency is very common in malaria endemic areas.
claims.source: Haemolysis can be life-threatening in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, which is very common in malaria endemic areas (Recht et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation.

claims.claim: Tafenoquine has been engineered to be much more stable than primaquine.
claims.source: Tafenoquine has been engineered to be much more stable than primaquine.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known property of tafenoquine's chemical design.

claims.claim: The contribution of oxidative metabolites to the pharmacological activity of tafenoquine is unclear.
claims.source: The contribution of oxidative metabolites to the pharmacological activity of tafenoquine is unclear (St Jean et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an uncertainty in the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The precise mechanism of action of 8-aminoquinoline antimalarials in killing hypnozoites remains unknown.
claims.source: Indeed, the precise mechanism of action of the 8-aminoquinoline antimalarials in killing hypnozoites remains unknown.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claims.claim: A single 300 mg dose of tafenoquine (approximately 5 mg base/kg) was chosen for phase 3 evaluation in adults following a phase 2b dose-ranging trial.
claims.source: Following a phase 2b dose-ranging trial, a single 300 mg dose of tafenoquine (approximately 5 mg base/kg) was chosen for phase 3 evaluation in adults (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact about the clinical development program, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The principal dose-limiting concern for tafenoquine was the haemolytic potential in G6PD deficient heterozygote females.
claims.source: The principal dose-limiting concern at the time was the haemolytic potential of tafenoquine in G6PD deficient heterozygote females (Rueangweerayut et al., 2017), who often test as 'normal' in G6PD deficiency rapid screens.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the rationale for dose selection, supported by citation.

claims.claim: G6PD deficient heterozygote females often test as 'normal' in G6PD deficiency rapid screens.
claims.source: The principal dose-limiting concern at the time was the haemolytic potential of tafenoquine in G6PD deficient heterozygote females (Rueangweerayut et al., 2017), who often test as 'normal' in G6PD deficiency rapid screens.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of rapid diagnostic tests.

claims.claim: The phase 3 tafenoquine registration trials showed approximate equivalence of 300 mg tafenoquine compared with lower dose primaquine (15 mg base daily for 14 days in adults).
claims.source: The phase 3 tafenoquine registration trials overall were interpreted as showing approximate equivalence of 300 mg tafenoquine compared with lower dose primaquine (15 mg base daily for 14 days in adults), although the pre-specified non-inferiority margin was not met, and in Southeast Asia, tafenoquine efficacy was significantly inferior to primaquine (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of published trial results, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The pre-specified non-inferiority margin was not met in the phase 3 tafenoquine registration trials.
claims.source: The phase 3 tafenoquine registration trials overall were interpreted as showing approximate equivalence of 300 mg tafenoquine compared with lower dose primaquine (15 mg base daily for 14 days in adults), although the pre-specified non-inferiority margin was not met, and in Southeast Asia, tafenoquine efficacy was significantly inferior to primaquine (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cited trial.

claims.claim: In Southeast Asia, tafenoquine efficacy was significantly inferior to primaquine in the phase 3 trials.
claims.source: The phase 3 tafenoquine registration trials overall were interpreted as showing approximate equivalence of 300 mg tafenoquine compared with lower dose primaquine (15 mg base daily for 14 days in adults), although the pre-specified non-inferiority margin was not met, and in Southeast Asia, tafenoquine efficacy was significantly inferior to primaquine (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cited trial.

claims.claim: P. vivax parasites from Southeast Asia and Oceania are considered to require higher 8-aminoquinoline doses for radical cure than elsewhere.
claims.source: P. vivax parasites from Southeast Asia and Oceania are considered to require higher 8-aminoquinoline doses for radical cure than elsewhere.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The World Health Organization recommends for adults a total primaquine dose of 420 mg base (30 mg daily) in Southeast Asia and Oceania compared with 210 mg (15 mg daily) in other endemic regions.
claims.source: The World Health Organization recommends for adults a total primaquine dose of 420 mg base (30 mg daily) in these regions compared with 210 mg (15 mg daily) in other endemic regions (World Health Organization, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a WHO guideline, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In the Southeast Asian region, the 300 mg adult dose of tafenoquine was inferior to a sub-optimal primaquine radical cure regimen.
claims.source: In the Southeast Asian region, the 300 mg adult dose of tafenoquine was inferior to a sub-optimal primaquine radical cure regimen, although the sample size was small (43 patients were randomised to low-dose primaquine, and 73 were randomised to tafenoquine 300 mg).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the clinical trials with sample size noted.

claims.claim: In the INSPECTOR trial, 300 mg single dose tafenoquine resulted in poor radical curative efficacy in Indonesian soldiers returning from Papua, Indonesia.
claims.source: In the recently reported INSPECTOR trial, 300 mg single dose tafenoquine resulted in poor radical curative efficacy in Indonesian soldiers returning from Papua, Indonesia, an area of high malaria transmission (Baird et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cited trial.

claims.claim: Papua, Indonesia is an area of high malaria transmission.
claims.source: In the recently reported INSPECTOR trial, 300 mg single dose tafenoquine resulted in poor radical curative efficacy in Indonesian soldiers returning from Papua, Indonesia, an area of high malaria transmission (Baird et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated as contextual information about the study location.

claims.claim: The single dose tafenoquine recommendation for all adults results in substantial variations in drug exposure because of variation in body weight.
claims.source: Although a single dose tafenoquine recommendation for all adults has practical advantages, because of variation in body weight, the single dose results in substantial variations in drug exposure.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about fixed dosing in variable weight populations.

claims.claim: The currently recommended adult dose of tafenoquine 300 mg is likely inferior to optimal primaquine regimens in preventing relapses of vivax malaria in all endemic regions.
claims.source: Taken together, it seems likely that the currently recommended adult dose of tafenoquine 300 mg is inferior to optimal primaquine regimens in preventing relapses of vivax malaria in all endemic regions (White, 2021; Watson et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the evidence, supported by citations.

claims.claim: 8-aminoquinoline drugs are considered to be pro-drugs.
claims.source: The 8-aminoquinoline drugs are considered to be pro-drugs, although there has been some debate about this for tafenoquine (St Jean et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated as general knowledge with a citation noting debate for tafenoquine.

claims.claim: For primaquine, plasma concentrations of the parent compound and the inactive carboxy metabolite can be measured readily.
claims.source: For primaquine, plasma concentrations of the parent compound and the inactive carboxy metabolite can be measured readily, but characterisation of the active metabolites, or their biotransformed derivatives, has proven challenging.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about analytical capabilities.

claims.claim: Characterisation of primaquine's active metabolites has proven challenging.
claims.source: For primaquine, plasma concentrations of the parent compound and the inactive carboxy metabolite can be measured readily, but characterisation of the active metabolites, or their biotransformed derivatives, has proven challenging.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claims.claim: Tafenoquine has a terminal elimination half-life of about 15 days.
claims.source: Tafenoquine has a terminal elimination half-life of about 15 days compared with 5 hours for primaquine, so capturing transient active metabolites is even more difficult.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known pharmacokinetic property.

claims.claim: Primaquine has a terminal elimination half-life of about 5 hours.
claims.source: Tafenoquine has a terminal elimination half-life of about 15 days compared with 5 hours for primaquine, so capturing transient active metabolites is even more difficult.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known pharmacokinetic property.

claims.claim: Increases in red cell methaemoglobin production following 8-aminoquinoline administration could be used as an in vivo pharmacodynamic proxy of oxidative antimalarial activity.
claims.source: We have suggested that increases in red cell methaemoglobin (MetHb) production following 8-aminoquinoline administration could be used as an in vivo pharmacodynamic proxy of oxidative antimalarial activity (White et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citation.

claims.claim: MetHb is an oxidation product in which the ferrous iron (Fe2+) of intraerythrocytic haem has been oxidised to the ferric form (Fe3+).
claims.source: MetHb is an oxidation product in which the ferrous iron (Fe2+) of intraerythrocytic haem has been oxidised to the ferric form (Fe3+).
claims.evidence: This is a biochemical definition.

claims.claim: Data from over 500 P. vivax malaria patients given high-dose primaquine radical cure suggested that increases in day 7 blood methaemoglobin concentrations were associated with greater radical curative efficacy.
claims.source: Data from over 500 P. vivax malaria patients given high-dose primaquine radical cure suggested that increases in day 7 blood methaemoglobin concentrations (which is approximately the day of peak methaemoglobinaemia in a daily primaquine radical cure regimen) were associated with greater radical curative efficacy (Chu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: Day 7 is approximately the day of peak methaemoglobinaemia in a daily primaquine radical cure regimen.
claims.source: Data from over 500 P. vivax malaria patients given high-dose primaquine radical cure suggested that increases in day 7 blood methaemoglobin concentrations (which is approximately the day of peak methaemoglobinaemia in a daily primaquine radical cure regimen) were associated with greater radical curative efficacy (Chu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cited study.

claims.claim: Efficacy data were pooled from 1073 patients with acute P. vivax malaria recruited in nine countries between October 2010 and May 2017.
claims.source: Efficacy data were pooled from 1073 patients with acute P. vivax malaria who were recruited in nine countries (Table 1) between October 2010 and May 2017 (Appendix 1—figure 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the study population and data collection period.

claims.claim: All patients were treated with a standard dose regimen of chloroquine (1500 mg base equivalent over 3 days).
claims.source: All patients were treated with a standard dose regimen of chloroquine (1500 mg base equivalent over 3 days) and were randomised to either single dose tafenoquine (varying doses), low-dose primaquine (15 mg base equivalent daily for 14 days), or to no 8-aminoquinoline treatment.
claims.evidence: This describes the treatment protocol in the trials.

claims.claim: In patients who received tafenoquine (n=634), single doses ranged from 50 mg to 600 mg.
claims.source: In the patients who received tafenoquine (n=634), single doses ranged from 50 mg to 600 mg, with weight adjusted doses ranging from 0.5 mg base/kg to 14.3 mg/kg (i.e. a greater than 25-fold variation of weight adjusted dose).
claims.evidence: This describes the dose range in the study population.

claims.claim: Weight adjusted tafenoquine doses ranged from 0.5 mg base/kg to 14.3 mg/kg, representing a greater than 25-fold variation.
claims.source: In the patients who received tafenoquine (n=634), single doses ranged from 50 mg to 600 mg, with weight adjusted doses ranging from 0.5 mg base/kg to 14.3 mg/kg (i.e. a greater than 25-fold variation of weight adjusted dose).
claims.evidence: This describes the weight-adjusted dose range in the study population.

claims.claim: Patient weight varied considerably across the nine countries, with the heaviest patients in Brazil (median weight 70 kg) and the lightest patients in Ethiopia and the Philippines (median weight 53 kg).
claims.source: Patient weight (and thus mg/kg tafenoquine dose) varied considerably across the nine countries, with the heaviest patients in Brazil (median weight 70 kg) and the lightest patients in Ethiopia and the Philippines (median weight 53 kg), see Appendix 1—figure 2.
claims.evidence: This describes geographic variation in patient characteristics.

claims.claim: A 0.7 mg/kg increase in the total primaquine dose was associated with an odds ratio for recurrence within 4 months of 0.72 (95% CI 0.66–0.78).
claims.source: A 0.7 mg/kg increase in the total primaquine dose was associated with an odds ratio for recurrence within 4 months of 0.72 (95% CI 0.66–0.78): a very similar dose effect for the two drugs.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of primaquine data.

claims.claim: The mean probability of recurrence at 4 months was 0.15 (95% CI: 0.10–0.23) following 5 mg/kg tafenoquine.
claims.source: Our model estimated that the mean probability of recurrence at 4 months was 0.15 (95% CI: 0.10–0.23) following 5 mg/kg tafenoquine and 0.17 (95% CI: 0.10–0.26) following 3.5 mg/kg primaquine.
claims.evidence: This is a model-based estimate from the statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The mean probability of recurrence at 4 months was 0.17 (95% CI: 0.10–0.26) following 3.5 mg/kg primaquine.
claims.source: Our model estimated that the mean probability of recurrence at 4 months was 0.15 (95% CI: 0.10–0.23) following 5 mg/kg tafenoquine and 0.17 (95% CI: 0.10–0.26) following 3.5 mg/kg primaquine.
claims.evidence: This is a model-based estimate from the statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The posterior probability that recurrence was more likely following primaquine than tafenoquine was 0.73.
claims.source: The posterior probability that the recurrence was more likely following primaquine was 0.73.
claims.evidence: This is a Bayesian statistical result.

claims.claim: The association between tafenoquine mg/kg dose and recurrence was observed in all three geographic regions (Americas, Horn of Africa and Southeast Asia).
claims.source: The association between tafenoquine mg/kg dose and recurrence was observed in all three geographic regions (Americas, Horn of Africa and Southeast Asia: Appendix 1—figure 3), with near identical results when using any recurrence by 6 months as the endpoint, or analysing by time to first recurrent event (Appendix 1—figures 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a result from subgroup analyses shown in figures.

claims.claim: No recurrences by 4 months were observed in any patients in the highest dosing group (≥8.75 mg/kg, n = 43).
claims.source: No recurrences by 4 months were observed in any patients in the highest dosing group (≥8.75 mg/kg, n = 43).
claims.evidence: This is an observed result from the data.

claims.claim: Taking 15 mg/kg as the maximum tolerated single dose of tafenoquine, a dose of approximately 7.5 mg/kg achieves 90% of the effect achieved with 15 mg/kg.
claims.source: Taking 15 mg/kg as the maximum tolerated single dose of tafenoquine, a dose of approximately 7.5 mg/kg achieves 90% of the effect achieved with 15 mg/kg (Appendix 1—figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a model-based prediction from the Emax model.

claims.claim: Under the Emax model, increasing the dose from 3mg/kg to 4 mg/kg reduces the mean estimated recurrence proportion from 28.5% to 20.8%.
claims.source: For example, increasing the dose from 3mg/kg to 4 mg/kg reduces the mean estimated recurrence proportion from 28.5% to 20.8%; increasing to 5 mg/kg gives a mean recurrence proportion of 14.2%.
claims.evidence: This is a model-based prediction from the Emax model.

claims.claim: Increasing the tafenoquine dose to 5 mg/kg gives a mean recurrence proportion of 14.2%.
claims.source: For example, increasing the dose from 3mg/kg to 4 mg/kg reduces the mean estimated recurrence proportion from 28.5% to 20.8%; increasing to 5 mg/kg gives a mean recurrence proportion of 14.2%.
claims.evidence: This is a model-based prediction from the Emax model.

claims.claim: A fixed 300 mg dose in an adult would result in a mean recurrence proportion of 15.3% (95% CI: 9.6–21.7).
claims.source: Using the empirical weight distribution from the three efficacy trials, we estimate that a fixed 300 mg dose in an adult would result in a mean recurrence proportion of 15.3% (95% CI: 9.6–21.7), whereas a 450 mg fixed dose would result in a mean recurrence proportion of 6.2% (95% CI: 3.2–11.5).
claims.evidence: This is a model-based prediction using empirical weight data.

claims.claim: A 450 mg fixed dose would result in a mean recurrence proportion of 6.2% (95% CI: 3.2–11.5).
claims.source: Using the empirical weight distribution from the three efficacy trials, we estimate that a fixed 300 mg dose in an adult would result in a mean recurrence proportion of 15.3% (95% CI: 9.6–21.7), whereas a 450 mg fixed dose would result in a mean recurrence proportion of 6.2% (95% CI: 3.2–11.5).
claims.evidence: This is a model-based prediction using empirical weight data.

claims.claim: The 300 mg fixed dose reduces recurrence rates by around 70%.
claims.source: Given that approximately half the patients with no 8-aminoquinoline treatment had a recurrence, this implies that the 300 mg fixed dose reduces recurrence rates by around 70%, whereas a 450 mg fixed dose would reduce them by around 85%.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the model predictions and observed recurrence rates.

claims.claim: A 450 mg fixed dose would reduce recurrence rates by around 85%.
claims.source: Given that approximately half the patients with no 8-aminoquinoline treatment had a recurrence, this implies that the 300 mg fixed dose reduces recurrence rates by around 70%, whereas a 450 mg fixed dose would reduce them by around 85%.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the model predictions and observed recurrence rates.

claims.claim: Increasing the adult dose from 300 mg to 450 mg would translate into a number needed to treat of 11 patients (95% CI 7–21) to prevent one additional recurrence of malaria.
claims.source: If the 300 mg adult dose was increased to 450 mg this would translate into a number needed to treat of 11 patients (95% CI 7–21) to prevent one additional recurrence of malaria (Appendix 1—figure 10) with the greatest absolute benefit for patients weighing over 60 kg (Appendix 1—figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is a calculated metric based on the model predictions.

claims.claim: A total of 4499 tafenoquine plasma concentrations in 718 individuals (72 healthy volunteers and 646 patients with symptomatic P. vivax malaria) were available for pharmacokinetic modeling.
claims.source: We fitted mixed-effects population pharmacokinetic models to all available plasma tafenoquine levels (a total of 4499 tafenoquine plasma concentrations in 718 individuals: 72 healthy volunteers and 646 patients with symptomatic P. vivax malaria).
claims.evidence: This describes the pharmacokinetic dataset.

claims.claim: The data were described adequately by a two-compartment elimination model.
claims.source: The data were described adequately by a two-compartment elimination model, consistent with previous analyses of these data (Thakkar et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a result from pharmacokinetic modeling, consistent with prior work.

claims.claim: In a model adjusted for tafenoquine mg/kg dose, Cmax was not significantly associated with recurrence (OR: 1.01 for a doubling in Cmax, 95% CI 0.69–1.49).
claims.source: The same pattern was seen for the Cmax: in a univariable model there was a strong association between Cmax and recurrence, but in a model adjusted for tafenoquine mg/kg dose this association was no longer significant (OR: 1.01 for a doubling in Cmax, 95% CI 0.69–1.49).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from multivariable analysis.

claims.claim: Dose administered rather than parent compound exposure was the main observed driver of therapeutic efficacy.
claims.source: Thus dose administered rather than parent compound exposure was the main observed driver of therapeutic efficacy.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analyses showing dose effects persist after adjustment for exposure.

claims.claim: Each additional mg/kg of tafenoquine was associated with a 19% (95% CI: 17% to 21%) increase in day 7 MetHb concentrations.
claims.source: Increases in blood MetHb concentrations following tafenoquine administration were highly correlated with the mg/kg dose (Figure 3a–c). Each additional mg/kg was associated with a 19% (95% CI: 17% to 21%) increase in day 7 MetHb concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of MetHb data.

claims.claim: Peak MetHb levels were observed around day 7 following tafenoquine administration.
claims.source: As reported previously for high-dose primaquine (Chu et al., 2021), peak MetHb levels were observed around day 7 (Figure 3a–b).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data, consistent with prior findings for primaquine.

claims.claim: Each absolute percentage point increase in the day 7 MetHb concentration was associated with an odds ratio for recurrence of 0.81 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.99) in a model adjusted for mg/kg dose.
claims.source: Adding the day 7 MetHb concentration as a linear predictor in the logit-Emax model (i.e. in a model adjusted for the mg/kg dose of tafenoquine), each absolute percentage point increase in the day 7 MetHb concentration was associated with an odds ratio for recurrence of 0.81 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.99).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from multivariable modeling.

claims.claim: After adjustment for the mg/kg dose, healthy volunteers had slightly lower day 7 methaemoglobinaemia compared to patients infected with P. vivax (15% lower, 95% CI: 0 to 34% p=0.02).
claims.source: Overall, after adjustment for the mg/kg dose, healthy volunteers had slightly lower day 7 methaemoglobinaemia compared to patients infected with P. vivax (15% lower, 95% CI: 0 to 34% p=0.02), Appendix 1—figure 13.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing healthy volunteers to patients.

claims.claim: Volunteers who received DHA-PQP had day 7 MetHb that was 23% lower (95% CI: 1.5 to 40%) compared with those volunteers who were not given a partner drug.
claims.source: When comparing by randomised arm in the healthy volunteer trial, the largest observed difference was in those who received DHA-PQP in whom the day 7 MetHb was 23% lower (95% CI: 1.5 to 40%) compared with those volunteers who were not given a partner drug.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from subgroup analysis.

claims.claim: Lumefantrine may inhibit cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6).
claims.source: Lumefantrine may inhibit cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) (Novartis Pharmaceuticals, 2021, see next section).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on a citation to pharmaceutical information.

claims.claim: Higher plasma lumefantrine concentrations were associated with lower day 7 MetHb levels (ten-fold increase in day 7 plasma lumefantrine concentration was associated with a 40% reduction in day 7 methaemoglobin (95% CI: 3 to 62%)).
claims.source: Higher plasma lumefantrine concentrations were associated with lower day 7 MetHb levels (ten-fold increase in day 7 plasma lumefantrine concentration was associated with a 40% reduction in day 7 methaemoglobin (95% CI: 3 to 62%), Appendix 1—figure 14).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of drug-drug interaction data.

claims.claim: For piperaquine there was no clear association with the day 7 MetHb concentrations (40%; 95% CI: –27 to 72%).
claims.source: In contrast, for piperaquine there was no clear association with the day 7 MetHb concentrations (40%; 95% CI: –27to 72%).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no significant association.

claims.claim: CYP2D6 metabolises primaquine to a series of bioactive hydroxylated metabolites.
claims.source: CYP2D6 metabolises primaquine to a series of bioactive hydroxylated metabolites (Camarda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about primaquine metabolism, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Genetic polymorphisms in CYP2D6 resulting in loss of function are associated with reduced primaquine radical curative efficacy.
claims.source: Genetic polymorphisms in CYP2D6 resulting in loss of function are associated with reduced primaquine radical curative efficacy (Baird et al., 2018; Baird, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: A total of 716 patients had CYP2D6 genotyping data.
claims.source: A total of 716 patients had CYP2D6 genotyping data, with a wide range of variants observed.
claims.evidence: This describes the genotyping data available.

claims.claim: The most common poor metaboliser alleles were *10 (10.5% allele frequency), *4 (5.8% allele frequency) and *5 (3.1% allele frequency).
claims.source: The most common poor metaboliser alleles were *10 (10.5% allele frequency), *4 (5.8% allele frequency) and *5 (3.1% allele frequency).
claims.evidence: This describes the genetic variant frequencies in the study population.

claims.claim: 34 (8.9%) patients randomised to tafenoquine had a predicted enzyme activity score of 0.5 or less (poor metabolisers).
claims.source: In the efficacy analysis population, of those randomised to tafenoquine, 34 (8.9%) patients had a predicted enzyme activity score of 0.5 or less (poor metabolisers) (Caudle et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes the prevalence of poor metabolisers in the study population.

claims.claim: There was no clear association between the 2D6 activity score and vivax malaria recurrence at 4 months following tafenoquine (OR for recurrence: 0.9 [95% CI 0.4 to 2.2] for poor versus normal/extensive metabolisers).
claims.source: Consistent with the previous analysis of these data (St Jean et al., 2016) there was no clear association between the 2D6 activity score and vivax malaria recurrence at 4 months following tafenoquine (OR for recurrence: 0.9 [95% CI 0.4to 2.2] for poor versus normal/extensive metabolisers), although statistical power was low as few patients had low activity scores.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result, consistent with prior analysis.

claims.claim: 2.3% (15/651) of patients vomited within 1 hour of oral tafenoquine administration.
claims.source: In total 2.3% (15/651) of patients vomited within 1 hour of oral tafenoquine administration.
claims.evidence: This is a tolerability outcome from the trials.

claims.claim: There was no clear association between vomiting and the mg/kg dose (OR for vomiting per mg/kg increase: 1.08 [95% CI: 0.88–1.32]).
claims.source: There was no clear association with the mg/kg dose (OR for vomiting per mg/kg increase: 1.08 [95% CI: 0.88–1.32]).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from tolerability analysis.

claims.claim: One patient treated with tafenoquine had a greater than 5 g/dL fall in Hb.
claims.source: One patient treated with tafenoquine had a greater than 5 g/dL fall in Hb, but no patients had a greater than 25% fall in Hb to <7 g/dL, or a fall to less than 5 g/dL.
claims.evidence: This is a safety outcome from the trials.

claims.claim: No patients had a greater than 25% fall in Hb to <7 g/dL, or a fall to less than 5 g/dL.
claims.source: One patient treated with tafenoquine had a greater than 5 g/dL fall in Hb, but no patients had a greater than 25% fall in Hb to <7 g/dL, or a fall to less than 5 g/dL.

results.result: The study pooled individual patient data from 1073 patients with P. vivax malaria and 72 healthy volunteers across multiple pre-registration trials, with tafenoquine doses ranging from 50-600 mg (0.5-14.3 mg/kg), representing a >25-fold variation in weight-adjusted dosing. A total of 4499 plasma tafenoquine concentrations were available for pharmacokinetic modeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C44-C48, and C64 describe the study population and data collection comprehensively. The numbers are internally consistent (1073 patients + 72 volunteers ≈ 1102 total mentioned in abstract), and the dose ranges and geographic variation are clearly documented with appropriate detail for a meta-analysis.

results.result: Tafenoquine dose (mg/kg) is the primary determinant of radical cure efficacy, with each additional mg/kg associated with an OR of 0.70 (95% CI: 0.65-0.76) for recurrence at 4 months. The dose-response relationship is steep around the currently recommended dose and was consistent across all three geographic regions (Americas, Horn of Africa, Southeast Asia).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C51-C54, C100, and C149 collectively demonstrate a clear, statistically significant dose-response relationship supported by logistic regression and Emax modeling. The consistency across geographic regions (C54, C149) strengthens the finding. The statistical evidence is robust with appropriate confidence intervals and the relationship holds in multiple analytical approaches.

results.result: Under an Emax model, the currently recommended 300 mg dose (5 mg/kg in 60 kg adult) achieves only 70% of maximal hypnozoiticidal effect, with predicted recurrence of 15.3% (95% CI: 9.6-21.7). Increasing to 450 mg would achieve 90% of maximal effect with predicted recurrence of 6.2% (95% CI: 3.2-11.5), translating to NNT=11 (95% CI: 7-21) to prevent one additional recurrence.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C56-C63 present model-based predictions from the Emax pharmacodynamic model. The estimates are internally consistent and appropriately qualified with confidence intervals. The NNT calculation (C63) follows logically from the predicted recurrence rates. However, these are model predictions requiring prospective validation, which the authors acknowledge in their recommendations (C155).

results.result: Increasing the tafenoquine dose to 7.5 mg/kg (450 mg) would result in 90% reduction in P. vivax recurrence risk and is predicted to more than halve recurrence rates at 4 months, averting one relapse per 11 patients treated, with greatest benefit in heavier patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C106-C107, and C156 present consistent model-based predictions for higher dosing. The 90% reduction claim (C5) aligns with the Emax model showing 7.5 mg/kg achieves 90% of maximal effect (C56). The predictions are appropriately qualified as estimates requiring prospective validation, though the wording in C5 could be misinterpreted as empirical rather than model-based.

results.result: After adjustment for dose, terminal elimination half-life and day 7 methaemoglobin concentration were associated with recurrence, but parent compound exposure (AUC, Cmax) was not. More rapid elimination (despite lower total exposure) was associated with increased efficacy, indicating that dose administered rather than parent compound exposure drives therapeutic efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C68-C69, and C113 describe multivariable regression results showing that pharmacokinetic parameters associated with metabolism (half-life, MetHb) predict efficacy after dose adjustment, while exposure metrics do not. This pattern is internally consistent and supports the metabolite hypothesis. The statistical analyses appropriately control for confounding by dose.

results.result: The production of oxidative metabolites is central to tafenoquine's hypnozoiticidal efficacy. Tafenoquine behaves pharmacologically like a slowly eliminated form of primaquine and requires metabolism for its pharmacological activity, with oxidative activity necessary for both radical curative activity and haemolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C112, C114, C118-C119, and C142 present the central mechanistic conclusion. This inference is well-supported by the convergent evidence: (1) dose matters more than exposure (C69), (2) faster elimination predicts better efficacy (C113), (3) MetHb correlates with efficacy (C74), and (4) the pattern fits the proposed causal model (C142). However, direct measurement of active metabolites is lacking (acknowledged limitation C129).

results.result: Methaemoglobin production is highly correlated with tafenoquine dose (19% increase per mg/kg, 95% CI: 17-21%), peaks around day 7, and is associated with radical curative efficacy (OR 0.81 per percentage point increase, 95% CI: 0.65-0.99) after dose adjustment. MetHb serves as a useful, non-invasive pharmacodynamic surrogate for radical curative activity, though it does not lie on the causal pathway to hypnozoite killing.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74, C115, C124, C140-C141 describe the MetHb findings comprehensively. The dose-MetHb correlation is strong and well-quantified (C72). The association with efficacy after dose adjustment (C74) is statistically significant though the confidence interval barely excludes 1.0. The interpretation that MetHb is a surrogate marker rather than causal mediator (C140) is appropriate and consistent with the causal model in Figure 4.

results.result: Tafenoquine pharmacokinetics were adequately described by a two-compartment elimination model. Since tafenoquine metabolites could not be measured directly, their production was inferred from parent drug elimination rate and pharmacodynamic properties were inferred from methaemoglobin concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C138-C139 describe the pharmacokinetic modeling approach and its limitations. The two-compartment model is consistent with prior analyses (C65 cites Thakkar et al., 2018). The inference approach (C138-C139) is clearly stated as a methodological limitation, which is appropriate given the inability to measure active metabolites directly.

results.result: Healthy volunteers had 15% lower day 7 methaemoglobinaemia than P. vivax patients after dose adjustment (p=0.02). Among healthy volunteers, those receiving DHA-PQP had 23% lower MetHb (95% CI: 1.5-40%) compared to no partner drug. Higher lumefantrine concentrations were associated with 40% lower MetHb (95% CI: 3-62%), while piperaquine showed no clear association.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 describe potential drug-drug interactions affecting MetHb production. The statistical associations are reported with appropriate confidence intervals. However, the interpretation is complicated by the inability to separate drug effects from disease effects when comparing patients to volunteers (acknowledged in text). The lumefantrine-MetHb association (C79) is intriguing but based on small sample size (n=24 per arm in phase 1 trial) and the mechanism via CYP2D6 inhibition (C78) is speculative.

results.result: Among 716 genotyped patients, 8.9% (34/382) receiving tafenoquine were CYP2D6 poor metabolisers (activity score ≤0.5). There was no clear association between CYP2D6 activity score and recurrence (OR 0.9, 95% CI: 0.4-2.2) or elimination half-life. The study was insufficiently powered to evaluate CYP2D6's role in tafenoquine bioactivation, though CYP2D6 appears to be a minor determinant of efficacy at the population level compared to dosing.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86, C143, C150-C153 describe the CYP2D6 analysis and its limitations. The lack of association (C86) is appropriately qualified as having low statistical power due to small numbers of poor metabolisers (C85, C151). The conclusion that CYP2D6 is a minor population-level determinant (C153) is reasonable given the low prevalence of poor metabolisers, but the study cannot definitively rule out an important role in the subset of poor metabolisers. The inference is limited by inadequate power rather than contradictory evidence.

results.result: Tafenoquine was generally well tolerated with 2.3% vomiting within 1 hour (no dose association). Severe haemolysis was rare: one patient had >5 g/dL Hb fall, none had >25% fall to <7 g/dL. Each mg/kg increase was associated with -0.02 g/dL Hb change (95% CI: -0.04 to 0.00, p=0.02), implying 300 mg in 60 kg adult causes ~0.1 g/dL reduction (<1% of Hb), and 450 mg would cause 0.15 g/dL reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 and C108 describe safety outcomes with appropriate quantification. The haemoglobin effects are small and clinically insignificant in G6PD-normal individuals. The statistical significance (p=0.02, C92) with confidence interval barely excluding zero suggests a real but minimal effect. The calculations for 300 mg and 450 mg doses (C93-C94) follow appropriately from the regression coefficient. However, these data are only for G6PD-normal individuals and cannot inform safety in G6PD-deficient patients.

results.result: Day 7 MetHb concentration was correlated with haemoglobin reductions on day 2-3 (1% MetHb increase associated with -0.08 g/dL Hb change, 95% CI: -0.12 to -0.03). Conversely, each day increase in elimination half-life was associated with +0.02 g/dL Hb (95% CI: 0.01-0.04). Tafenoquine causes minor oxidative haemolysis in G6PD-normal individuals that correlates with methaemoglobinaemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96, C116-C117 describe relationships between MetHb, half-life, and haemolysis that are internally consistent with the oxidative metabolite hypothesis. The opposing directions of effect for MetHb (negative) and half-life (positive) on haemoglobin align with the model where faster metabolism produces more oxidative metabolites. The statistical associations are appropriately quantified with confidence intervals. These findings support the causal model in Figure 4.

results.result: The currently recommended adult dose of tafenoquine is insufficient for radical cure in all adults, with heavier patients particularly disadvantaged by fixed dosing. Substantial improvements in radical curative efficacy are possible with small dose increases. The results allow accurate characterisation of the tafenoquine dose-response relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C101-C102, and C154 present the main clinical conclusion. This is well-supported by the steep dose-response curve (C100), the Emax modeling showing current dose achieves only 70% of maximal effect (C4), and the consistency across geographic regions (C149). The disadvantage for heavier patients (C101) follows logically from fixed dosing with steep dose-response. The characterisation is based on the largest dataset available (C112 notes this comprises majority of all tafenoquine trial data).

results.result: Prospective studies should assess tolerability, safety and efficacy of higher tafenoquine doses. Much larger doses (up to 2100 mg over one week) have been studied previously. The only severe haemolytic reaction occurred in a G6PD-deficient heterozygote receiving 1200 mg over 3 days; a homozygote receiving the same dose had 3 g/dL Hb drop but remained asymptomatic.
results.evaluation: Claims C155, C109-C111 present the recommendation for future studies with supporting safety context. The recommendation (C155) follows logically from the finding of suboptimal current dosing. The historical safety data (C109-C111) from cited studies provides context that higher doses have been tolerated, though the severe reaction in a heterozygote (C110) highlights the continued concern for G6PD-deficient individuals. This appropriately frames the need for careful dose-escalation studies.

results.result: The steep dose-response relationship explains the poor results in the INSPECTOR trial, where Indonesian soldiers (mean weight 70 kg, heavier than registration trial patients) received fixed 300 mg dose in a high-transmission setting (Papua). High transmission (heavier hypnozoite burdens) and lower mg/kg dosing likely contributed substantially to poor efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 and C31 provide a retrospective explanation for the INSPECTOR trial results using the current study's findings. The explanation is internally consistent: heavier patients (C126) receiving fixed dose get lower mg/kg dosing, which combined with high transmission (C127) and the steep dose-response curve (C100) would predict poor efficacy. This demonstrates the clinical relevance of the dose-response findings, though it remains a post-hoc explanation rather than a prospective prediction.

results.result: The two major study limitations are absence of direct metabolite measurements and imprecision in measuring relapse. Genotyping was limited to three microsatellite loci without probabilistic relapse/reinfection assessment. However, studies were in low-transmission settings and 83% (298/360) of recurrences occurred within 4 months, making reinfection contribution unlikely. The similar 4-month and 6-month endpoint results suggest future studies could use 4-month follow-up.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C137 comprehensively describe study limitations and their mitigation. The authors appropriately acknowledge the inability to measure active metabolites (C129) and limitations in distinguishing relapse from reinfection (C130-C132). The argument that reinfection is unlikely (C133-C134) is reasonable given low transmission settings and timing of recurrences. The recommendation for 4-month follow-up (C135) is pragmatic and supported by the data (C136-C137), though this represents a change from traditional 6-month endpoints.

results.result: Only DETECTIVE part 1 randomised patients to different doses; other studies had dose variation from weight variation. Patient weight was not associated with recurrence, and over half of weight variation is polygenic (unlikely related to malaria risk). The dose-recurrence relationship was consistent across all three geographic regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 address potential confounding in the dose-response analysis. The concern that weight-based dose variation could be confounded by weight-related malaria risk factors is appropriately addressed by: (1) lack of weight-recurrence association (C147), (2) polygenic nature of weight variation (C148), and (3) consistency across regions (C149). The authors also note nearly identical results when analyzing only the randomised dose-ranging trial (DETECTIVE part 1), though this is mentioned in text rather than as a formal claim.

results.result: For primaquine, a 0.7 mg/kg dose increase was associated with OR 0.72 (95% CI: 0.66-0.78) for recurrence at 4 months, similar to tafenoquine's dose effect. No recurrences occurred in the highest tafenoquine dosing group (≥8.75 mg/kg, n=43).
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C55 provide comparative context for tafenoquine's dose-response. The primaquine comparison (C50) validates that the observed tafenoquine dose effect is of similar magnitude to the established comparator drug. The zero recurrences in the highest dose group (C55) supports the dose-response relationship, though the sample size (n=43) is relatively small and confidence intervals would be wide.

results.result: Tafenoquine is a newly licensed 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial, the first new drug for radical treatment of relapsing malaria in 70 years. It is eliminated slowly and can be given as single-dose radical cure or weekly chemoprophylaxis, providing substantial operational advantage over primaquine which requires daily dosing for 7-14 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C13 provide background context about tafenoquine's regulatory status and clinical positioning. These are well-established facts supported by the cited registration trials (C11-C12) and comparative pharmacology (C13). This contextual information appropriately frames the study's importance.
